title: What is momentum investing?
hook: Buy what's working. Exit what isn't. Let rules decide.
slides: The idea
Stocks that have outperformed over the past 6 to 12 months have tended to keep outperforming for a while.
Not prediction
Momentum doesn't forecast the future. It follows what prices are already doing, and respects it.
How it's done
Rank a universe of stocks by past returns, hold the strongest, and replace laggards at every rebalance.
Rules, not opinions
The edge comes from following the ranking consistently, especially when it feels uncomfortable.
takeaway: Momentum is a disciplined way to ride strength, not a guess about what's next.

title: Why does momentum work?
slides: Under-reaction
Investors are slow to absorb good news. Prices adjust gradually, creating trends.
Herding
Once a trend is visible, more investors join it, extending the move.
The disposition effect
People sell winners too early and hold losers too long, which slows price discovery in both directions.
Why it persists
These are human habits. As long as markets are run by people, they tend to repeat.
takeaway: Momentum exists because investor behaviour is predictable, even when prices aren't.

title: The evidence for momentum
hook: One of the most studied effects in finance.
slides: The classic study
Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) showed that US stocks with the best 3 to 12-month returns kept outperforming over the following months.
Everywhere
Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen (2013) found momentum across countries and asset classes, in 'Value and Momentum Everywhere'.
In the textbooks
Carhart (1997) added momentum to the standard factor model used to evaluate fund managers.
In India
NSE runs dedicated momentum indices, such as the Nifty200 Momentum 30, now tracked by index funds and ETFs.
takeaway: Momentum has decades of research behind it, across markets and asset classes.

title: A rule-based momentum framework
hook: Four rules that turn an idea into a system.
slides: 1. Universe
Start with liquid stocks (for example, the top 200 or 500 by size) so trades are easy to execute.
2. Ranking
Rank by risk-adjusted return over 6 and 12 months. Adjusting for volatility avoids chasing only the wildest stocks.
3. Rebalance
Review on a fixed schedule (monthly or quarterly): add new leaders, exit stocks that have dropped down the ranks.
4. Risk control
Size positions sensibly and use a market filter (for example, the index vs its 200-day average) to manage exposure.
takeaway: A momentum strategy is only as good as the rules you follow every single rebalance.

title: Momentum's weak spot: crashes
hook: The risk every momentum investor must respect.
slides: What happens
After a sharp bear market, beaten-down stocks often rebound fastest. Momentum portfolios, full of former winners, can lag badly.
It's documented
Daniel and Moskowitz (2016) studied these 'momentum crashes', which tend to come at market turning points.
Managing it
Regime filters, volatility-based sizing and diversification across factors can soften the blow.
The trade-off
Higher long-run returns come with deeper, sharper drawdowns. Size momentum as a part of the portfolio, not all of it.
takeaway: Momentum pays for its returns with occasional sharp crashes. Plan for them.

title: Value vs Growth
hook: Two styles, two very different bets.
slides: Value
Buys companies that look cheap on earnings, book value or cash flow, betting the market has been too pessimistic.
Growth
Buys companies with fast-rising sales and earnings, accepting higher valuations for faster expansion.
They take turns
Value and growth leadership swings over multi-year cycles, often with interest rates and the economic cycle.
Where momentum fits
Momentum isn't tied to either. It owns whatever is leading, value or growth.
takeaway: Value and growth take turns; momentum simply follows whichever is leading.

title: The quality factor
slides: What it is
Quality stocks have high profitability, low debt and stable earnings.
Why it works
Strong businesses tend to keep compounding, and investors often under-price that durability.
The evidence
Novy-Marx (2013) showed profitable companies have earned higher returns, linking quality to value investing.
When it shines
Quality has often held up better in downturns: a defensive factor that still grows.
takeaway: Quality is the factor of resilience: compounding with fewer nasty surprises.

title: The low-volatility puzzle
hook: Why calmer stocks have often done surprisingly well.
slides: The theory
Classic finance says more risk should mean more return.
The reality
Low-volatility stocks have often delivered returns similar to the market with smaller swings, the 'low-risk anomaly'.
Why
Many investors chase exciting, lottery-like stocks and overpay for them, leaving steady stocks under-owned.
The catch
Low volatility usually lags in sharp bull runs. Its strength shows up in falls.
takeaway: Low volatility trades upside excitement for a smoother ride, and that has often paid.

title: Factors take turns
slides: Rotation
Momentum, value, quality and low volatility each lead in different market phases.
The trap
Investors switch to last year's best factor, just in time for it to cool off.
Multi-factor
Combining factors that behave differently (like momentum and value) has historically smoothed returns.
Stick with it
Each factor needs years to show its edge. Patience is part of the strategy.
takeaway: Diversify across factors, and give each one time to work.

title: Two kinds of momentum
slides: Cross-sectional (relative)
Ranks stocks against each other and owns the strongest, whatever the market is doing.
Time-series (absolute)
Looks at each asset's own trend: own it when it's rising, step aside when it's falling. Also called trend following.
Using both
Relative momentum picks the leaders; absolute momentum decides how much to have invested at all.
Why it matters
Combining them can keep you in strong markets and reduce exposure in long declines.
takeaway: Relative momentum picks what to own; absolute momentum decides how much to own.
